Being Wrong Productively

Fallibilism as an operating system

State in advance what would change your mind. Everything else is decoration.

2 min read3 figures, each sourcedWhere it is contestedUpdated 21 September 2026
On this pageBy the numbersHow it happenedWho did the workWhere it is contestedWhat I changed my mind aboutGo to the sourceReads across to

The useful question is never 'am I right' — it's 'what would I expect to see if I weren't, and have I actually looked'.

If you keep one line

Say in advance what would change your mind — precisely enough that you can't renegotiate later.

ShareEmailXLinkedIn

Popper's contribution was to move the demarcation line. A theory earns scientific status by forbidding something — by being exposed to a test it could fail. Naive falsificationism doesn't survive contact with real science: Duhem and Quine pointed out you can always rescue a theory by adjusting an auxiliary assumption, and Lakatos and Kuhn showed working scientists do exactly that, often correctly, for years at a time. But the underlying discipline survives all of it. Say in advance what would change your mind, and say it precisely enough that you can't renegotiate later.

Feynman's 1974 Caltech address gave the operational version. Cargo cult science has all the outward form — the papers, the apparatus, the vocabulary — and is missing 'a kind of leaning over backwards' to report everything that might make you look wrong, including the alternatives you considered and rejected and why. He was describing experimental integrity. It reads now as a description of most public argument.

The replication crisis is what the failure mode looks like at scale. The 2015 Reproducibility Project attempted 100 psychology studies; of the 97 with significant original effects, 36% replicated significantly. Not fraud, mostly — just a system in which every local incentive rewarded a positive result and nothing rewarded checking. The fix that worked best was boring and procedural: pre-registration, which is Popper's rule turned into paperwork.

The practical apparatus is small and unglamorous. Hold beliefs with explicit confidence rather than binary conviction. Write predictions down before outcomes, because otherwise you will reconstruct your reasoning and remember having been right. And distinguish 'I was wrong about the conclusion' from 'I was wrong about the process' — only the second should update how you think, and it's the one people skip.

01By the numbers

1934Popper's Logik der Forschung — falsifiability as demarcation (the title page reads 1935): Wikipedia, 'The Logic of Scientific Discovery'
1974Feynman's 'Cargo Cult Science' commencement address: Richard Feynman, 'Cargo Cult Science', Caltech, 1974 (Caltech Archives)
36%Of 97 significant psychology findings, the share that replicated significantly: Open Science Collaboration, 'Estimating the Reproducibility of Psychological Science', Science 349(6251), 2015

02How it happened

  1. 1934Popper's 'Logik der Forschung' proposes falsifiability as the line between science and everything else.
  2. 1962Kuhn's 'Structure of Scientific Revolutions' describes what scientists actually do, which is not that.
  3. 1974Feynman's 'Cargo Cult Science' address: the ethic, stated operationally.
  4. 2011Simmons, Nelson and Simonsohn publish 'False-Positive Psychology' and name researcher degrees of freedom.
  5. 2015The Reproducibility Project: 36% of 97 psychology findings replicate significantly.
  6. 2015–Pre-registration and registered reports spread — Popper's rule as an administrative form.

03Who did the work

Karl PopperMoved the question from 'how do we confirm theories' to 'how do we expose them'.
Richard FeynmanTurned the epistemology into an ethic you could actually follow on a Tuesday.
Brian NosekRan the Reproducibility Project and built the infrastructure that made pre-registration routine.

04Where it is contested

Popper's falsificationism is not the consensus philosophy of science it's usually invoked as. Kuhn, Lakatos and Feyerabend all argued that scientists rightly protect promising theories from refutation for long stretches, and that a field abandoning every theory at the first anomaly would abandon all of them. Treat it as a personal heuristic, not a criterion.

05What I changed my mind about

I used to deploy 'that's unfalsifiable' as a conversation-ender. It's a weak move: almost nothing interesting is cleanly falsifiable in isolation, because you're always testing a bundle of assumptions at once. The stronger and more annoying question is 'what specific observation would move you, and by how much'.

07Reads across to

John Snow — the founding case of the method, and the founding case of a story told better than the evidence supports.

Vasily Arkhipov — a story the world believes, and the document that would settle it, which has not appeared.

The Heated Disk — why the rule is harder than it sounds: what meets the evidence is a bundle, never one claim on its own.

The Plastic Tide — the rule under field conditions, where the honest answer is still that nobody knows yet.

Charles Darwin — twenty years spent hunting whatever would sink it, which is what the rule looks like with someone behind it.

Edward O. Thorp — the rule with money on it: state the edge in advance, because the bet size is computed from the number you claimed.

Forty-Two — the same rule approached from the failure side: the answer survives, the question does not, and nobody notices until it is acted on.
